# Bigmart Sales Data Set using machine learning for beginners

Retail industry uses analytics to optimize business processes. Tasks like product placement, inventory management, customized offers, product bundling, etc. are being smartly handled using data science techniques. 


```{r include=FALSE}
DF <- read.csv(file="bigmart_data.csv", sep = ",", dec='.')
hist(DF$Item_Outlet_Sales)

nb_Prod <- length(unique(DF$Item_Identifier))
nb_Outlet <- length(unique(DF$Outlet_Identifier))

```

## Variables description

+ `Item_Identifier` : Unique product ID
+ `Item_Fat_Content` : Whether the product is low fat or not
+ `Item_Type` : The category to which the product belongs
+ `Outlet_Identifier` : Unique store ID
+ `Outlet_Size` : The size of the store in terms of ground area covered
+ `Outlet_Location_Type` : The type of city in which the store is located
+ `Outlet_Type` : Whether the outlet is just a grocery store or some sort of supermarket

+ `Item_Weight` : Weight of product
+ `Item_Visibility` : The % of total display area of all products in a store allocated to the particular product
+ `Item_MRP` : Maximum Retail Price (list price) of the product
+ `Outlet_Establishment_Year` : The year in which store was established
+ `Item_Outlet_Sales`: Sales of the product in the particular store. This is the outcome variable to be predicted.


## Problem: Predict the sales of a store


The data are collection of `r dim(DF)[1]` sales data for `r nb_Prod` products across `r nb_Outlet` stores in different cities. 
Also, certain attributes of each product and store have been defined. The aim is to build a predictive model and find out the sales of each product at a particular store.

Using this model, we will try to understand the properties of products and stores which play a key role in increasing sales.

## The Hypotheses

Here we draw some hypotheses on the potential determinants of the products demand.

*Store Level Hypotheses:*

+   **City type**: Stores located in `urban` or `Tier 1` cities should have higher sales because of the higher income levels of people there.
+   **Population Density**: Stores demand should be positively associated with population density.
+    **Store Capacity**: Stores capacity should act as an attracting factor and rises demand.
+    **Competitors**: Stores competitive environment should have negative effect on sales.
+    **Marketing**: Stores which have a good marketing division should have higher sales as it will be able to attract customers through the right offers and advertising.
+    **Location**: Stores located within popular marketplaces should have higher sales because of better access to customers.
+    **Customer Behavior**: Stores keeping the right set of products to meet the local needs of customers will have higher sales.
+    **Ambiance**: Stores which are well-maintained and managed by polite and humble people are expected to have higher footfall and thus higher sales.

*Product Level Hypotheses:*

+    **Brand**: Branded products should have higher trust and then sales.
+    **Age of the product**: Time on the market should help positive reputation and image building.
+    **Packaging**: Good packaging can attract customers.
+    **Utility**: Higher quality products should have higher utility and sale.
+    **Display Area**: Products on bigger shelves in the store should sell more.
+    **Visibility in Store**: The location of product in a store will impact sales.
+    **Advertising**: Better advertising of products in the store will should higher sales in most cases.
+    **Promotional Offers**: Products accompanied with attractive offers and discounts will sell more.


## Data exploration

### First we search for missing values. 


We found two variables with missing values – `Item_Weight` and `Outlet_Size.` Lets impute the former by the average weight of the particular item. 

### Second we reduce item type (`Item_Type`) to 3 categories only: *Food, Drinks and Non-Consumables*

The `Item_Type` variable has 16 categories which might prove to be very useful in analysis. So its a good idea to combine them. One way could be to  assign a new category to each.
`Item_Identifier`, i.e. the unique ID of each item, it starts with either `FD`, `DR` or `NC`. It like being Food, Drinks and Non-Consumables. 
 
### Third we correct some typos in `Item_Fat_Content`


There are typos and difference in representation in categories of `Item_Fat_Content` variable.

There were some non-consumables as well and a fat-content should not be specified for them.

```{r}
# Item_FAt_Content
DF %>% select(Item_Fat_Content) %>% table
DF <-  dplyr::mutate(DF, 
              Item_Fat_Content = case_when(Item_Fat_Content %in% c("LF","low fat","Low Fat") ~ "Low Fat",
                                           Item_Fat_Content %in% c("reg","Regular") ~ "Regular"))
DF$Item_Fat_Content <- factor(DF$Item_Fat_Content)
table(DF$Item_Fat_Content)
# Item_Type
table(DF$Item_Identifier)
DF <- DF %>% mutate(DF, 
              Item_Type2 = case_when( str_detect(Item_Identifier, "DR") ~ "Drink",
                                       str_detect(Item_Identifier, "FD") ~ "Food",
                                       str_detect(Item_Identifier, "NC") ~ "Non Consommable"))
DF <- DF %>% separate(Item_Identifier, c("Item_Type2", "Item_Id"), sep = 2)
table(DF$Item_Type, DF$Item_Type2 )

## Counting the freq for each character var

var_freq_plot_fn <- function(df){
  purrr::map(df %>% select_if(is.character) %>% names, ~
  df %>% 
    count(.data[[.x]]) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = n, y = .data[[.x]], fill = .data[[.x]])) +
    geom_col() +
    theme(legend.position = "none"))
}

var_freq_plot_fn(DF)
```


```{r}
## Counting NA for each var

NA_count_fn <- function(df){ 
  df %>% select(everything()) %>%  # replace to your needs
  summarise_all(funs(sum(is.na(.)) / length(.)))
}
NA_count_fn(DF)

# Average imputation for Missing `Item_Weight`
DF <- DF %>% 
  group_by(Item_Type2) %>% 
  mutate(Av_weight = mean(Item_Weight, na.rm=T)) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(Item_Weight2 = ifelse(is.na(Item_Weight),  Av_weight, Item_Weight))

sum(is.na(DF$Item_Weight2))
```
# Data Formating

## Categorical data

```{r}
DF$Item_Type2 <- factor(DF$Item_Type2)
DF$Item_Fat_Content <- factor(DF$Item_Fat_Content)
DF$Outlet_Establishment_Year <- factor(DF$Outlet_Establishment_Year)
DF$Outlet_Size <- factor(DF$Outlet_Size)
DF$Outlet_Location_Type <- factor(DF$Outlet_Location_Type)
DF$Outlet_Type <- factor(DF$Outlet_Type)
```


# Regression analysis
## Simple regression

Let start with simple regression model.
First we evaluate one variable impact on the sales. Justify your choice of explanatory variable and perform and discuss the regression.


```{r}
my.cor <- DF  %>% select_if(is.numeric) %>% select( -Item_Weight, -Av_weight) %>% cor
corrplot::corrplot(my.cor)
```


```{r}
Reg1 <- lm(data=DF, Item_Outlet_Sales ~ Item_MRP)
summary(Reg1)
```

This regression shows significant correlation between sales and price (as expected). We can use these results as benchmark to evaluate the following regressions

### Regression diagnostic

```{r}
sp <- ggplot(DF, aes(x=Item_MRP, y=Item_Outlet_Sales)) + 
  geom_point(colour="grey60") +
  stat_smooth(method=lm,  colour="black")
sp
```

```{r}
plot(DF$Item_Outlet_Sales ~ DF$Item_MRP)
abline(Reg1, col='red')
```



```{r}
plot(Reg1)
```

```{r}
ggplot(DF,aes(Item_MRP, Item_Outlet_Sales)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method='lm'
              #, se=FALSE
              ) 
```


## Multiple regression


### Regression with quantitative variables:

```{r}
library(ggforce)

ggplot(DF, aes(x = .panel_x, y = .panel_y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  ggforce::facet_matrix(vars(Item_Outlet_Sales , Item_MRP , Item_Visibility ,  Item_Weight2), layer.diag = 4)
```

```{r}
Reg2 <- lm(data=DF, Item_Outlet_Sales ~ Item_MRP + Item_Visibility +  Item_Weight2)
summary(Reg2)
```


### Searching for Outlet impact on sales

Let discuss the regression of sales on establishment year, size and type of outlet. Comment regression results.

```{r}
Reg3 <- lm(data=DF, Item_Outlet_Sales ~ Outlet_Establishment_Year + Outlet_Size + Outlet_Type)
summary(Reg3)
```


```{r}
table(DF$Outlet_Size, DF$Outlet_Type)
```

### Mixing with Item variables

```{r}
Reg4 <- lm(data=DF, Item_Outlet_Sales ~ Item_Fat_Content + Item_Type2)
summary(Reg4)
```
```{r}
Reg4 <- lm(data=DF, Item_Outlet_Sales ~ Item_MRP * Item_Type2)
summary(Reg4)
```



## Prediction

Using the first regression model : `Reg1`: `Item_Outlet_Sales ~ Item_MRP` we can predict sales for new data: new values of `Item_MRP`

```{r}
Reg1 <- lm(data=DF, Item_Outlet_Sales ~ Item_MRP)
summary(Reg1)
```


```{r}
new.data <- data.frame(Item_MRP = c(mean(DF$Item_MRP), median(DF$Item_MRP)))
#predict(Reg1 , new.data)
new.data2 <- data.frame( Item_MRP =   seq(min((DF$Item_MRP), max(DF$Item_MRP))))
predict(Reg1,  new.data2 ,interval = "prediction")
newDF <- data.frame(Item_MRP = DF$Item_MRP)
pred1 <- as.data.frame(predict(Reg1,  newDF, interval = "prediction"))
names(pred1) <- c( "Item_Outlet_Sales", "lower", "upper")

```

### Make prediction for: an average product (average in terms of size, etc.) belonging to the type low fat.

```{r eval=FALSE}
# example that can be modified
predict(lm(y ~ x), new, se.fit = TRUE)
pred.w.plim <- predict(lm(y ~ x), new, interval = "prediction")
pred.w.clim <- predict(lm(y ~ x), new, interval = "confidence")
matplot(new$x, cbind(pred.w.clim, pred.w.plim[,-1]),
        lty = c(1,2,2,3,3), type = "l", ylab = "predicted y")
```


```{r}
ggplot(DF, aes(DF$Item_MRP, Item_Outlet_Sales)) +
geom_point()+
  facet_wrap(~ DF$Item_Type2)+ geom_line(data = pred1, lwd =2 , colour='red')

```
